newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's opposition vows to intensify protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's opposition vows to intensify protests.

text.p: Bulgarian opposition parties vowed to intensify nation-wide strikes and protests on Tuesday after ruling Socialists defiantly unveiled a new government instead of bowing to pressure to call early elections.
Nikolai Dobrev, nominated to be prime minister, will hand the names of his proposed cabinet to President Petar Stoyanov on Tuesday. A confidence vote will be held in parliament on Wednesday.
Despite open divisions in the party over whether to cling to power or call elections, a Socialist assembly approved the draft cabinet by 150 votes to seven.
The Socialists suffered a crushing defeat in presidential elections in November, prompting prime minister Zhan Videnov to resign amid heavy criticism over his handling of the economy.
The economy is staggering under debts. Inflation is 50 percent a month. The International Monetary Fund and European Union have said there will be no help until a stable government is in place.
The determination of the Socialists, the country's former communists, to form a government has provoked widespread strikes, protests and transport disruption over the past week.
"We will not give up," said Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces which has held 29 days of mass rallies to press for elections nearly two years ahead of schedule.
The campaign, and rising civil disobedience, have gained momentum since the Socialists received a mandate from Stoyanov to form a new government last week.
Bulgaria's land links to Greece, Romania and the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia have been cut for several days with long queues of commercial trucks trapped at the roadside.
Mass rallies have been held daily in Sofia and dozens of other cities and towns to demand elections and to condemn the economic policies of the Socialists.
In Sofia long queues formed outside bread shops on Monday, with people stocking up before inflation sends prices higher.
Hundreds of students blocked Sofia's main roads throughout the day and vowed to keep up their action on Tuesday. Students danced, sang and sported badges which said: "No Left Turn".

The airport closed for an hour and union officials warned all traffic could be stopped from Thursday. Miners, dockers, teachers, students, pensioners have all gone on strike or taken to the streets around Bulgaria in recent days.
The anti-government campaign has built into one of the biggest protests since the end of communist rule in 1989.
In naming his proposed cabinet, largely unchanged from the previous Socialist government, Dobrev said a one-party cabinet was regrettable but better than no cabinet at all.

National police chief Hristo Marinsky, well aware of recent clashes between anti-government protesters and police in former Yugoslavia, appealed to Stoyanov and politicians to find a way of keeping the daily protests peaceful.
But Dobrev, the powerful interior minister in the outgoing cabinet, warned to protesters against civil disobedience, which has increased dramatically over the past week.
He said: "Peaceful protests are understandable but civil disobedience is outside the law, especially in a country with hyperinflation."

Asked whether he would use of force if there was a repeat of a January 10 siege of parliament by opposition supporters, he said "I would have no choice" but added "I am not, however, a bloodthirsty vampire".
